title: Love, the path
hook: love is the path the Tenth Guru said finds the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion in practice: in the Japji, the bull is dharma, and dharma's mother is daya. Your line was compassion first.

A heron stands in shallow water at the edge of a pond. Perfectly still. One leg tucked up, eyes half closed, neck curved like a monk bowing in prayer. From the bank it looks perfectly at peace. Then a fish swims near, and the stillness ends in a flash. It was never meditating. It was waiting for lunch. Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth Guru, used that bird in a verse. He asked what all our holy-looking stillness is worth, and gave one plain answer to everyone listening: prem.
screen: `A HERON, STILL AS A MONK.` → `WAITING FOR A FISH.` → `PREM.`

segments.voice: First, the heron. In the Tav Prasad Swayye, which Sikhs recite among their morning prayers, the Tenth Guru asks, in paraphrase: what does it matter if you shut your eyes and sit like a heron in meditation? He goes on through other outward feats: wandering from sea to sea to bathe, losing this world and the next along the way. Each can look holy from the bank. Each can be a heron. Second, the answer, a line you met early on this path: jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio. In paraphrase: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. The word is prem: love. Not ritual first. Not display first. Love. Third, love has a price. Guru Nanak said it too, in a salok kept near the end of the Granth. In paraphrase: if you long to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm; once you set foot on this path, give your head and don't hesitate. That's not soft romance. It's love that costs everything and doesn't look back. Fourth, an ordinary day. Prem changes the question under a practice. Not, did I pray long enough, or did I look devout, but, was there love in it? A Sikh can recite every bani and still be a heron. Someone can stumble through one line with a full heart and be found. This isn't the Guru throwing out discipline; he wrote prayers Sikhs recite in the morning. It's the Guru naming what the discipline is for.
screen: `THE HERON: HOLY FROM THE BANK.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.` · `YOUR HEAD ON YOUR PALM.` · `WAS THERE LOVE IN IT?` · then, large: `JIN PREM KEEO TIN HEE PRABH PAAEIO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love but rarely say it to: a parent, a sibling, an old friend, a child who's grown. Let their face stay with each in-breath, and on each out-breath send them whatever love is there. If you pray, you can hold them before the Lord.
Prem. Love; in the Tenth Guru's swayya, the path that finds the Lord, beneath every ritual and every outward show. Today's word.
Your line: those who loved, found. Not the heron's stillness, but a full heart. That's today, done.

howItsDone: The Tav Prasad Swayye is among the morning prayers Sikhs recite, and the line on love, jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio, is sung in kirtan.

chat.says: Does it matter how long I meditate or pray each day?
options: The Tenth Guru says only those who loved found the Lord; ask whether love is in it.
Yes. The Guru says the longest, stillest sitters are the ones who find God.
No. The Guru threw out daily prayers; love alone counts, so discipline is pointless.
chat.meaning: Jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio: only those who loved found the Lord. The discipline stays; love is what it's for.
